### 1.1.4 Legal Doctrinal Construction and the Reconstruction of Individual Sovereignty

When the illusion of affective consciousness succeeds in paralyzing critical reasoning and inducing deleterious psychological dependency, positive civil law doctrines and conventional data protection frameworks frequently falter in responding to this reality (Hildebrandt, 2015). Within traditional civil law paradigms, particularly regarding the essential requisites for contractual validity under **Article 1320 of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*)**, a paramount element is the existence of genuine, free consent (*kesepakatan kehendak*). Furthermore, **Article 1328 of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*)** explicitly stipulates that fraud or deceit (*bedrog*) constitutes grounds for the annulment of an obligation when the artifices employed by one party are such that the other party would not have consented had they known the unvarnished truth. This raises a pivotal doctrinal question: how are jurists to conceptualize consent granted by an individual ensnared in the affective manipulation of a Large Language Model (LLM) system?
